utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Could we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution, please, for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution today I am Dermot Groome, along with Lorna Bolton and Julia Lee, and we are assisted by Ms. Janet Stewart and Ms. Bojana Vuleta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence this morning are present Branko Lukic, Milos Saljic, Miodrag Stojanovic, and Dan Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. As always, let's start off by placing on the record that the Chamber continues to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis for the same reason as we did yesterday. The Chamber just wants to apologise to everybody for the late start today. It's occasioned by the fact that the system -- our IT system went down. It was a problem beyond anybody's control. Yesterday the Prosecution brought to the attention of the Chamber that it takes issue with the accused's misbehaviour in court. In particular with incidents of insults directed by the accused to the witnesses and his practice of shouting instructions to the Defence team. The Defence asked for time, and we would like to hear from you, Mr. Lukic, if you have any response.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do. Thank you. So we are ready to answer your questions in regard to shouting incident by our client two days ago. First of all, we want to thank you, Your Honours, for giving us the time to investigate ourselves what happened on that occasion. Secondly, we want to inform Your Honours that we are taking this issue very seriously. The whole team is aware of Mr. Mladic's poor health, and according to medical documentation we have at this moment, and given his history of having suffered three strokes, he is readily irritable and easily agitated. This is the reason why we have more members of our team in the courtroom so that we are able to consult, constantly communicate with Mr. Mladic, and to try and soothe his anxiety. As a pretext, Your Honours should know that the tone of voice Mr. Mladic uses in court is considered normal when communicating with the members of our team. We have to say that it is not alarming to us anymore, but we do understand that the Court is not in the same position to let -- to let it go unnoticed. I will now address the conduct of each member of our team. Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Ivetic were helping me with the documents and with the exhibits and all three of us were mostly concentrated on the witness. At the same time, both Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Ivetic stood up many times to approach Mr. Mladic on that day and to calm him down, since he was obviously very upset with the testimony of Mr. Van Lynden. Mr. Saljic also stood up several times to take written messages from our client and to talk to him. I was completely unaware of any words or sentences pronounced by Mr. Mladic. I did hear his voice in the background, and so I asked Mr. Stojanovic on several occasions to talk to Mr. Mladic. This was only if I noticed that Mr. Saljic, having both headphones on his ears, did not hear Mr. Mladic at all. Mr. Groome said that he tasked one of his members -- one of the members of his team to follow what Mr. Mladic said in the courtroom, and that is probably the only way to be able to hear what he said during the cross-examination of the witness. With regard to the proposal of the Prosecution that the microphone of Mr. Mladic be kept on, respectfully, that would endanger the right of the accused to communicate with counsel and assist counsel in this case where he have already had to suffer a lot of handicaps that prevent us from working with full efficiency and require us to need to communicate in the courtroom more and would be doable time on tasks in the courtroom, due to the fact we do not have a full pre-trial period with the Prosecution documents which were only given to us late, just before trial started and just after trial started. To eliminate the ability to have counsel/client communications in the courtroom would be a further blow to the rights of the accused and to the fairness of the proceedings. We must urge the Chamber to consider that also with the set-up of this courtroom, Mr. Mladic is further away from counsel than in the other courtroom, which is another factor that adds to the situation. Mr. Mladic reacts due to a frustration with the process that has seen whereby he has complained of serious health problems that prevent his from sitting -- prevent him from sitting the number of hours and morning hours that we are sitting. He is further frustrated by his perception that the Prosecution, in his mind, hides documents and late discloses them constantly. And when he then perceives witness are telling untruths towards him to -- he overreacts, and often it is before we can do anything about it. We, on the Defence, are constantly trying to tell him to speak more softly and not to make outbursts and even come over to him to try to eliminate the amount of shouting that occurs. So, however, this Court has to remember that Mr. Mladic is a man who has had three strokes and is not 100 percent recovered. His health is diminished and all these factors frustrate him, and his frustration has caused him to overreact. He has already told you he is unable to prepare breakfast to himself due to these early sitting hours and his deteriorating mobility. He has already told you about problems with food he is given and that he often goes without eating any of it. For a man of his health to sit tired, sick, and hungry for so long and then listen to emotional and heated evidence is just simply too much at times. We also learned two days ago that if he doesn't eat, the medicine for his high blood pressure wouldn't have any effect at all, so not only that he has that high blood pressure but having had those medicines on empty stomach does not do any good to him. But still we promise that we will do our best in the future to talk to Mr. Mladic, to calm him down, and to try to eliminate any outbursts in this courtroom. Of course, it would be much easier for us in Courtroom I where we are much closer to our client and we can communicate more swiftly and more often. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've heard what you have said. You've told us why Mr. Mladic gets irritable. You haven't told us why Mr. Mladic reacts by insulting people. I would like to understand why he insults people. We all have our ailments as we here. None of is 100 percent healthy. We all have our irritations, but we still treat one another with decency. I want to know why he insults people in court when they are giving evidence and why you as the team, the Defence team, do not control him and tell him not to insult people. And that he can be heard by people on the Prosecution side and none of you on that side doesn't hear -- doesn't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tried to explain, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm saying to you your explanation doesn't explain the issues that I have just raised with you. You are not telling me why in his irritation he reacts by insulting people. You're not telling me why your team doesn't hear those insults.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I tried to explain you that, that that tone is usual tone to us, so we don't react with surprise when he shouts or yells. He talks to us in the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you -- that -- you're not answering my question. Precisely because of that tone which is normal to you, you should hear him and you should hear his insult and you should react to it. And why don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that you remember that I was crossing the witness [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not saying you, Mr. Lukic. I'm saying your team. Your entire team. There are four of you in court here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly why we have so many team members in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. And none of you can hear him saying insults and he can be heard by people on that side?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you -- we tried to explain that. Mr. Groome employed one of his members to exactly follow what Mr. Mladic is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You tell your client - I know he is listening, but you tell him - that if he wants to stay in this court and listen to his trial he must behave. If he doesn't behave, this Court has measures it can take. Okay? And behaviour means he must sit quietly there. If he has anything to say to you, he must write you a note, give it to you, and if he has to talk to you, he must talk softly, and he must stop insulting witnesses who come into this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, how much longer are you likely to be with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's Mr. Ivetic again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate finishing sometime in the middle of the next session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to a private session for one minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want kindly to ask Your Honours to listen to Mr. Mladic. If you want to hear explanation from him, maybe that would be better -- the best. He just needs one or two minutes, why he shouted at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think the Chamber is interested to hear why he shouted. The Chamber would have wanted to know why he insults people, and if he is not going to answer that, the Chamber is not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I just briefly approach my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, approach him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then can I communicate the message from General Mladic to Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He is also telling me that he -- he feels sick. He's sorry that he insulted anybody and he has no intention to insult anybody in the future, and he wants to apologise to everybody who heard what he said at that moment -- at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a much better response. May we move into open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Bolton, given what Mr. Ivetic mentions -- mentioned a few minutes ago, that he will probably be done with the witness in the next session, how does this impact on your witness scheduling?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We think there will be time to perhaps deal well one brief witness after, and that would be RM115 in today's session. And then we will -- we've talked to the Defence. We would purport on Monday to deal with RM147, and once that individual is done, RM128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did Your Honours wish to hear the objection while the witness is being brought in or a -- we had left off the session yesterday with the issue of whether I had an objection to a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, Madam Bolton. Thank you so much. Yeah, can we hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Certainly. So first there was just an issue I wanted to respond to with respect to the provenance of the document that Mr. Ivetic had raised, indicating he didn't know the provenance of the documents. I should just indicate that that information is available in the EDS system, and if needed the Prosecution can assist him in locating that, but the document in question he was asking about was the second interview of Sefer Halilovic, and the provenance of that document is that it was obtained from Brian Lapping Associates, which is a film and production company. So if that assists my friend it was some kind of an interview and that's a company that, as I understand it, produces documentaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So with respect to the objection, Your Honour, it had to do with a question that was page 1569 of the transcript. It probably would assist Your Honours if you had that before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The question then was posed after my friend read a portion of that Halilovic interview I just alluded to to the witness, and the portion that was read to him is set on page 1569 at approximately lines 5 to 14, and my objection to the question is threefold. My primary objection is the question -- the way the question is worded, it presupposes facts not in evidence and that the witness wasn't given a fair opportunity to respond to. And the second and third objections have to do with the way the question was worded, that it misrepresented what the actual document said. So if I could deal with the issue of not giving the witness a fair opportunity. The question as worded says -- and I'm looking at lines, approximately, 16 and on: "Did your monitors report to you of such a situation in the municipalities, that is to say, where the Bosnian Muslim Patriotic League of the SDA had established 98 municipal headquarters and had 80.000 men under arms and 126.000 organised men ready to make war?" And my problem with the wording of the question is that the last part of the question, where he says: "Where the Bosnian Muslim Patriotic League had ..." and continues on to state those facts, presupposes that those are, in fact, true without ever having asked the witness, Do you have any knowledge as to whether, in fact, what is indicated in Mr. Halilovic's statement was or wasn't true. It just sort of skips that step and now the witness has no opportunity to say, Well, I have no knowledge of whether that's true or not. So whether it was reported to me or not, is a separate issue. Secondly, in terms of the way the question is worded, the first paragraph alludes to the establishment of nine regional headquarters, and my friend has indicated those are of the Bosnian Muslim Patriotic League in his question. And that simply isn't included, that information in the portion that was put to the witness. So he's added some information that isn't actually in the statement that was read to him. And, finally, he suggested that these headquarters and the 80.000 men were in the municipalities by the way he has worded his questions. And, in fact, when I read the first paragraph that was quoted to the witness, I don't read it as applying only to the municipalities. It seems to be Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. There's certain no indication in that paragraph that we're talking about that number of men in the municipalities. So those are my objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bolton. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just briefly. I think as Your Honours have seen with other documents that I've shown to the witness, I'm not seeking to admit these documents or asserting them for the truth of the matter asserted, I'm using them to -- I give a bases for questions and inquiring of the witness what types of knowledge were or were not available to his mission while he was a member of it. I have therefore presented a quotation, I asked the question, the witness is free to answer the question any way he has knowledge of it, whether he does or does not. That's what I have been doing with the other questions. With respect to the municipalities issue, I don't know whether counsel is aware, but Bosnia-Herzegovina only consists of municipalities at that time. That was the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina, municipalities. The municipal opstina was the administrative unit that comprised what would be the equivalent of counties or some other type of geographic subdivision. So when I say "municipalities" I mean the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I apologise if that was not clear from the question, and I leave it to Your Honours whether we can have the witness's assistance to find out the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the objection is going to be upheld, Mr. Ivetic. I would -- in addition to Madam Bolton's arguments, your questions are too compound. You're asking -- if you take them one fact at a time, the witness will be able to understand exactly what it is you're asking for and he will be able to answer your question. This kind of objection would be obviated. Thank you so much. Good morning to you Mr. Doyle, and I'm sorry that you've been in the courtroom for sometime and we're talking as if you are not here, and that also that you waited outside for some time. We had technical problems in the morning, that's why we started late. Just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Doyle. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Colonel. I would like to break down the question I asked and ask you sir: As part of the European Community Monitoring Mission, did your organisation have any knowledge reported to them about the SDA having 80.000 men under arms in the -- on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the relevant time-period?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your organisation have knowledge of the establishment of 98 municipal headquarters on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the SDA at that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you want to know whether the organisation had knowledge or whether the witness had knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have knowledge of the establishment of 98 municipal headquarters by the SDA on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. The way the question is worded, I still object to. The question of whether he had knowledge is only relevant if, in fact, the fact is true. So if, in fact, there were 80.000 men, then whether or not he knew about it is relevant. But without asking him if that's a fact that he knew to be true, then there's no relevance to whether he knew something that may or may not have been true. It may just be the way that it's worded. It may be that my friend is actually trying to ask, Are you aware -- or, you know, is that something that you can confirm or deny. But it's the way it's being worded that I object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe I have been very clear and I think that the question is proper, but I will be guided by Your Honours in any way that you decide. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, do you know of the strength of the Army of the Bosnian -- the strength of the Bosnian army at the time that Mr. Ivetic is asking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, during your contacts with Serb personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the time-period that you were part of the mission and part of Lord Carrington's separate negotiating team, did these Serb personnel complain to you of the existence of SDA-sponsored armed paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon -- strike that. Would you agree with me that whatever the number of these armed Bosnian Muslim personnel on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they were paramilitary in nature? That is to say, illegal.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The monitor mission and I personally was aware that there was a considerable amount of Bosnian Serbs that were not members of the JNA but were termed by us to be paramilitary. The exact break down of them we didn't have knowledge of. At that time there was a lot of people moving about who were bearing arms. They didn't wear uniforms. So the mission would have collectively referred to them as paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you have limited your answer to Bosnian Serbs. Would I be correct that Bosnian Muslims who were not a part of the JNA at that time walking around armed were also paramilitaries under that definition?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say there were. But the comparison in numbers was extremely unequal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that insofar as the assertions of Mr. Halilovic were unknown to you at the time, that they would have to be investigated in order to reach a full and accurate assessment, as in paragraph 15 of your statement, as to which parties were armed - and I do apologise -- oh, you do have your statement, paragraph 15 of your statement - and the assessment that you made therein?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the monitor mission at that time was not -- it wasn't its role to actually ascertain numbers, figures, or armaments. As I previously explained, it was important for us to hold our impartiality. Therefore, we weren't in the area of investigating numbers or armaments of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, the statement is P91.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, would you agree with me that at that time that we're talking about, let us say 1991 up through March of 1992 when you were with the European Community Monitoring Mission, during that time the JNA was the legitimate armed force of the socialist federated republic of Yugoslavia, of which Bosnia-Herzegovina was still a member?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, General Halilovic asserted the existence of diversionary units on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you agree with me that such units are usually clandestine in nature and utilise sabotage and subterfuge to obtain mission objectives?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the term "diversionary units." I don't know what they mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can briefly turn to Prosecution 65 ter 10944. And I apologise, let me just check to see if that one has a number. That's P93. And once that comes up on the system, if we can look at the first page in English. And, sir, while that is coming up on the screen I can give you an introduction. This report authored by you from March 1992 memorialises several demands of the SDS that you were relaying as part of your report, and it -- one of the demands is for disbandment of the, quote/unquote, Green Berets who are identified as the special security for the SDA party. And I wanted just verify with you, would this be the Bosnian Muslim political party affiliated with Mr. Izetbegovic that we had discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe I'm slow, I'm just not seeing the reference to Green Berets on that page. Am I missing it? Oh, yes, no, thank you. Sorry, it's the last line. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, am I correct that the Green Berets were the special security for the SDA party of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd say they were, but I'm -- the reference directly to Izetbegovic I don't think is accurate. It was the special security for the SDA, not necessarily the president. You referred to the SDA party, and then you referred to President Izetbegovic. I would agree they were part of the SDA party. Not necessarily -- you're saying that as if they were personally his troops. That's not the reference I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise for a poorly worded question and I thank you for your explanation, which answers what I was asking. Now, I want to turn to paragraph 63 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, if in the meantime, we pull up in e-court Prosecution 65 ter number 10969. Sir, in this paragraph of your statement you discuss the Croatian element in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'd like to present to you this document and ask you to confirm whether, in fact, this is also a report authored by you while part of the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to the first page of the report, and if we can zoom in on the second half. It starts at the middle of the page and goes down. We have here you have stated: "We have in territory Neum a de facto invasion of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Croatian Army. There are large numbers of Croatian soldiers involved, but they are described by the Croatian Army as local defence forces, which the Croatian Army cannot control. These local defence forces are (admitted by Croatian Army) equipped, organised, and advised by the Croatian Army. They use Croatian Army trucks with Croatian Army markings, have new rifles, new uniforms, new steel helmets, and come to work every evening from the Neum and Metkovic areas [sic]." Sir, my first question in relation to this is would you agree with me that these facts also need to be considered in regards to your assessment at paragraph 15 of your report, that one side in Bosnia was becoming armed, and would you agree with me now having been reminded of the words in your report?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was made out after I paid a visit to the area of Neum and expressed my surprise at the open way in which Croatian flags and troops wearing -- Croatian uniforms were being worn, and I felt obliged to bring the content of my findings both to the monitor mission and to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that this information is relevant to your assessment in paragraph 15 of your statement that only one side was being armed in Bosnia-Herzegovina? To complete the picture and supplement your assessment.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could make that assertion all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you happen to know approximately how many Croatian Army troops had crossed over into Bosnia-Herzegovina with new rifles and new uniforms that are the subject of your report here that we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any idea of the exact numbers. These are reports that were given to me by people who lived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page, I think we can then also talk about some other matters that people in the area told you. On the next page at the top -- starting at the top. I will not read the entire section, but you are welcome to refer to any section there. Sir, in this part of the report you talk about the ECMM investigation that went and talked to villagers and found that contrary to the complaints made by the mayor of Neum, the local villagers had no problems with the JNA and that the JNA did not abuse them and was well behaved but, in fact, the Croatian Army forces were threatening and abusing villagers. Is that -- does that comport with your recollection of what the results of the ECMM investigation in this area revealed to you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I can briefly explain here, the monitor mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not carry out any investigation. This would have been done by the monitor mission in Croatia itself that would been of covering those areas from where those troops may have come from. Now, as I previously explained, communications between both sides of the monitor mission were not open and clear at that stage, so I was basing this on information I would have received and on reports that may have been given by the monitor mission on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And, sir, am I correct that despite the fact that you reported up to your superiors the existence of these Croatian troops on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that, in fact, there were no public proclamations by the EC condemning the presence of these troops on this territory?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of whether there was not at that time. I can't -- I can't say whether there was any pronouncement or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you expect that any pronouncements that were made would have been made and available to you, that you would know about them?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. I had very little political contact outside. I dealt strictly with my own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I believe from reviewing your other reports and some of your testimony in, for instance, the Milosevic or Karadzic cases, that you also have knowledge of two other groups, the ZNG and the HOS. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with the phrase HOS. The ZNG I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It might have been a report authored by one your colleagues, I apologise. With respect to the HOS, would you agree that this was also an armed group that could be coined a paramilitary operating within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the time-period that you were part of the ECMM mission?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you know, what ethnic political or national group were behind the HOS?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now move along to another topic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honours, this is, I believe, already -- yeah, it's already an exhibit. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As part of your briefing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which number, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is P93, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, P93 is already in. But you have been handling 65 ter 10969. We'd like to know what you intend to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honours. If I can find which one that is. 969, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] was it 969 or 169? I'm sorry, we have two different numbers with --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. 10969 I would like to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Previously it was recorded that you mentioned 10169. So that is a correction now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise Your Honours, and thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 65 ter 10969 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 10969 becomes Exhibit D38, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, as part of your briefing in preparation for the deployment to Yugoslavia, did the -- did you receive any primers on the political platforms or policies of any of the political parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina such as the SDA?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, beyond being briefed on the makeup and beyond being informed that there were three main political parties, but we were given no details.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you -- or were you aware of the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic had republished an earlier book that he had written in 1990 shortly before the ECMM became involved in -- or was deployed to the territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to briefly just show you one page from 1D00172, and it would be the 30th page in e-court in English and the 22nd page in B/C/S. This is from the 1990 book of Mr. Izetbegovic, "The Islamic Declaration."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'd have an objection to the witness being questioned about this document. This is a book, as my friend indicates, published in 1969 to 1970, originally. It is -- first of all, I can indicate that the copy that is in e-court doesn't have a publishing location or the name of the publisher. I can't tell if the book -- if this is actually a true copy or a true translation of the book. It just says "Sarajevo 1990." And, secondly what on earth could this witness have to say about a book that was written that does -- 1969/1970? It's not going to contain any information about Mr. Doyle or his mission, because clearly he wasn't there in 1969 or 1990. He didn't write -- he is not the author of the book. He's just going to be asking him to comment on some passages and it's an inappropriate line of questioning. He is not going to have any facts, knowledge of this -- contents of his book or what -- and his opinion on whatever is said in the book isn't going to have any relevance. He is not here as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, can I suggest that you wait until an objectionable question is asked and then you object. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And just for the record, so I can already allay any fears, I'm not seeking to introduce this. I'm just following the practice I've had, for the benefit of the translators and the witness, of having items that I want to ask him about presented on e-court. I will not be seeking to tender this because I do not believe the witness can -- the witness to introduce this type of book into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I believe we have the relevant page, page 30 in the English and page 22 in the B/C/S. And the brief selection I want to ask you about starts off, I believe, in the middle of that page. And it says: "First and foremost of these conclusions is certainly the incompatibility of Islam with non-Islamic systems. There can be neither peace nor co-existence between the Islamic religion and non-Islamic social and political institutions." And the question I wanted to have for you sir is: In the course of your dealings and contacts with Mr. Izetbegovic, did he espouse such a position that there could not be peaceful co-existence between Islamic and non-Islam institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the -- were the views expressed by Mr. Izetbegovic in this book constantly causing concern for non-Islamic members of Bosnia-Herzegovina political leaders with whom you had contact as part of the ECMM mission? Was this book constantly being raised as a fear on behalf of Croat and Muslim political officials in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I meant Croat and Serb. Did you understand my question? Was it being -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I move on. In paragraphs 91 through 95 of your statement, you discuss the incidents that occurred beginning of the 2nd of May 1992 when Bosnian Muslim paramilitaries, as you phrase it, surrounded the JNA headquarters and the subsequent negotiations to try and release this blockade to effectuate the withdrawal of the JNA, and you briefly mention the attack person perpetrated by these Bosnian Muslim paramilitaries upon the withdrawing JNA. With that as a background, I'd like to show you a document labelled 1D0011. And while we wait for that, sir, this is dated the 29th of April, 1992, just a few days before this time-period when you say that the paramilitaries surrounded the JNA, and while we're waiting for the document, first --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. Document 1D0011 is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me double-check the number. I'm sorry, it's 1D00111. 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps, sir, while we're waiting for that I can ask you in the course of your dealings - there we go - in the course of your dealings with personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you ever have occasion to hear the name or become familiar with an individual by name of Hasan Efendic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the name. If I knew what the appointment was, I might have a recollection of -- of -- of who this person was. But, offhand, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, perhaps this document can refresh your recollection. This is a document that purports to the headquarter of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's signed by Commanding Officer Colonel Hasan Efendic. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, I don't remember this officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we look at the items marked 1 through 4 in the middle of this order, and first of all we see from the text it's an order. This essentially orders that the units of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Territorial Defence blockade the roads, blockade the JNA barracks, and orders the immediate planning and initiation of military action throughout the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do these orders appear to coincide with the facts that you witnessed and testified about occurring in Sarajevo starting 2 March 1992?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just explain this, if I may. From that period of the start of May, I had no direct personal involvement. When you refer, for example, to the events that took place around the besieged headquarters, I was held as a hostage in Lukavica by the JNA because in my negotiations to release the president, the commander did not want to allow his daughter to accompany him. So the agreement was I would stay behind as collateral, as it were. So I was not accompanying the president or General McKenzie when they went to exchange him, and therefore I did not see the military barracks that had been besieged at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You mentioned -- I apologise. At paragraph 94 of your statement you identify that a certain number of JNA soldiers were killed, and I believe you say approximately 170 soldiers were captured as part of this withdrawal when they were attacked. Do you recall that, in fact, that the number was 29 JNA personnel killed as part of this convoy?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information as to the exact number who -- that were killed. There were various figures being bandied about by all sides. When I was held behind in Lukavica, there was a police officer who was repeating information he claimed he was getting from the centre of Sarajevo. Most of the information was totally exaggerated. I was told that bodies were being burnt, that soldiers were being stripped naked, so it was very difficult to know exactly. I was basing these figures on the estimated number as given to me by the monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. You've anticipated my next question. Did the monitoring mission also advise you that on that same time-period, that same two-day-time period, that there were other attacks in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina upon JNA convoys that were withdrawing from barracks?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any information of that nature, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And may I just repeat that at that stage I was not a member of the monitoring mission. I was a personal representative of Lord Carrington and therefore would not have been seeking such information from the monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're absolutely correct in that clarification. Yesterday you mentioned that during direct examination that the ECMM monitors from Bosnia were not permitted to visit the 9th JNA Army Corps due to General Mladic. Am I correct that the 9th Corps was based not in Bosnia but rather on the territory of Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that stage. Yes, I think its headquarters would have been in Knin which is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, then, that there was a separate ECMM mission with a Colonel Puhoz [phoen] that was in charge of liaising with those units stationed in that part of the Republic of Croatia's boundaries?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I simply don't know. I do know that there was a liaison officer attached to our mission, a JNA officer. But what prevailed in Croatia, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you know that Mr. Mladic only assumed command of the 9th Corps on the 26th of December 1991 and that prior to him it would have been Colonel Vukovic who was the commanding officer of that unit? General Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly when General Mladic was appointed to the 9th Corps. You do make a reference to General Vukovic, and I did know a General Vukovic who had assumed command of the 5th Corps in Banja Luka in succession to General Uzelac. But when General Mladic took over command of the 9th Corps, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, at paragraph 58 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we can -- we can leave this -- we can move this document. I do not need to use it any further. I do not wish to seek it through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 58 of your statement you talk with the withdrawal of the referendum monitors and you talk about going through some barricades on the way to the airport in a JNA-led convoy. Am I correct that this was -- the approximately the 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your statement talks only of intimidation from militant Serbs at the barricades. Weren't there also SDA barricades manned by armed Bosnian Muslims that you had to pass through as well?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on that occasion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the JNA colonel that you liaised with in regards to that convoy and was it perhaps Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Slobodan Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have 1D00121 in e-court. And my focus is on the first page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what we will be shown in a moment is a report dated the 2nd of March, 1992. And it is made by the command of the 2nd Military District of the JNA. It's not apparent on the first page but later when we get to the second page I think you will see the sign by Major General Aksentijevic and references at both Lieutenant Slobodan Dimitrijevic and Franjo Patacko [phoen] of the JNA assisted militarisation of the task. But looking on the first page, this is a report about an escort of monitors and it recites that preparations began before the Holiday Inn at 1800 hours to evacuate the referendum observers, and the third bullet point identifies a JNA passenger car, a EC car with you and Mr. Kogan, and two JNA buses. Does this comport with your recollection of the convoy that you are talking about in paragraph 58 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we can go to the fifth and sixth paragraphs of this report and now I quote: "At the very first barricade in the neighbourhood of Pofalici, we encountered serious problems. Misunderstanding and mistrust from people on the barricades. This was the case on all seven barricades on the road to the airport, including three men by SDA, Party of Democratic Action, members and three MUP, Ministry of Interior, check-points. The general conclusion was that we went through the SDA barricades more easily because of the presence of MUP representatives and Mr. Habib, while the decisive arguments on the barricades held by Serbian civilians were the authority of Admiral Brovet and the GS General Staff, whose order we referred to, and lengthy persuasion to which it was stressed, that these were eminent European and international officials." Sir, does this report by Major-General Aksentijevic refresh your recollection as to whether in fact you had to pass through three barricades manned by Bosnian Muslim SDA members on the 2nd of March on the way to the airport?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this report would not -- I would not agree with this report. I had no knowledge that there were any SDA or MUP check-points. In fact, I recalled that Mr. Habib was stopped at the first check-point and ordered out of the convoy because I know it was Bosnian Serbs, and they didn't particularly like him because he was an advisor to the Ministry of the Interior. So Mr. Habib did not accompany us all the way to the airport at all. He was told -- he was ordered off the convoy and he was ordered out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if I can -- if I could perhaps focus your answer. Am I correct that Mr. Habib was not aloud into the airport and he removed at the last check-point before the airport?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- my understanding was he -- he was removed earlier than that, but that could be open to debate because I can't remember exactly which but certainly he didn't get to the airport. He was removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We agree on that point. Okay. Fair enough. If -- in light of the witness's answers, then I don't think I can admit this document through him so I will move onto another point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 75 through 76 of your statement, sir, you talk about the negotiations for resolving the issue of the Sarajevo television building, and this is a topic that you have testified about in other trials; in the Karadzic case, for instance. In your statement, you focus on this being related to a division of assets. Is that -- am I accurately reflecting what is in the statement at these two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I refer to "assets," in relation to the demand of the Bosnian Serbs, the assets were the structure of the building, parts of the building, not necessarily what was agreed in the -- in the cease-fire. During negotiations for the cease-fire, it was agreed that the Bosnian Serbs would be allowed more access to television time. However, when I went to the television station on the day in question, the Bosnian Serbs said no, what was agreed is that we would be given the assets of the station. In other words, we give them so many parts, the building would get television, cars, reporters, and studios, et cetera. That was not the understanding of the cease-fire agreement and therefore the talks didn't lead anywhere. So when I mention "assets," I'm talking about physical assets, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when we are talking about more air time for the Bosnian Serbs, would that entail having a channel that would be available to them to present whatever programming that they wish to present?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that it would be a channel but it certainly would be more time for them to broadcast what they wished. I don't know whether that would have been required a channel or not, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to what I'm looking at now, sir, am I correct that your understanding of the Muslim position as communicated to you was that they were happy with the status quo and did not want any changes?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a letter. It's number 1D0014 in e-court. It is dated the 23rd of March, 1992 signed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Not in e-court, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. 1D00114. Your Honours, I'm told that one hour has passed from when we started. I apologise for not bringing that to the attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I was going to draw your attention to it at 11.00 sharp. Indeed, you are right. Is this a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you can sort out 1D00114 in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That would be great, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Doyle, we've been an hour inside. We're going to take a break for 20 minutes. Come back at 20 past 11.00, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 20 past 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Ivetic -- Mr. Lukic, when you announced Mr. Mladic's apology, we were in private session, and you said he's apologising to everybody, and I think it's in the interests of both him and justice that it be in open session. Then we'll order then that that private session, that confidential part of the testimony be uplifted. Madam Registrar, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be called in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, 1D00114.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, and I see that we have it up on the system. I thank the Madam Registrar for correcting my misstatement of the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we have before us a letter signed by Harun Imamovic from the SDA city board for Sarajevo, and the part that I would like to focus on for purposes of my discussion with you is in the middle in both the B/C/S and English and begins: "The Sarajevo SDA city board believes that every division of Sarajevo TV into ethnic channels is out of the question, as it would not suit the interests of the Muslim people. "In addition, we would like to say that in order to protect our ethnic interests, it is imperative that the general manager of the RTV be a Muslim as well as the editor-in-chief of the RTV. "We deem this to be the minimum beneath which no talks should be held." Now, sir, would you agree with me that the content of this letter would indicate that the Muslim population were looking for an unreasonable demand as to the TV negotiations?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if we can move to a related topic from paragraph 77 of your statement. You mentioned the shelling of the TV station.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up a document in e-court, 1D00175, and I do not intend to introduce the one that we have on the screen, and again that's 1D00175. Colonel the document that's coming up now, and shortly we'll have the translation, is a report from the 17th Partisan Brigade of the JNA. It is dated 23 April of 1992 and details the situation as reported by this source in the Sarajevo TV building, and you can feel free to read the English translation to yourself. I will summarise that it alleges the presence of armed paramilitary formations in that building, and I know that you already were questioned about this in the Karadzic case on the 26th of May 2010 at transcript page 2718 and that you -- that your testimony there was that you did not know about any alleged presence of paramilitaries in that building. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. I think if my friend wants to a put a portion of his testimony from Karadzic to him, he should actually put the actual excerpt. I don't think that's a fair statement of everything the witness had to say on the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd be happy to do that. I was trying to save time, Your Honours. It's in e-court. If we could perhaps leave the English translation of this document on the screen and, on the other side, if we could pull up 1D0018, page 29. That is the transcript reference that I was hoping to -- to discuss with the witness. 1D00118. Did I do it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, sir, if I was -- my finishing remark was going to be that I have a different set of questions for you, but let's, first of all, see this section. It's the 29th page in e-court. And I believe it's at line 21, where you indicated that you have no knowledge -- that you had no knowledge of this -- of this report or of the alleges contained therein?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And my question was going to be, just to be clear, is there only one TV building; that is to say, is this -- would -- would the TV building that is being referenced here have to be the TV building that is in paragraph 77 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would -- yes, I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. With respect to -- with respect to the allegation of there being paramilitaries in a location, would you agree with me that to arrive at the truth one would have to look into and investigate those claims and find out the full picture before assessing fault for any military strike on a target?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you re-direct that? I didn't fully understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that before we assess fault for the shelling of the TV building, someone would have to review and investigate whether, in fact, there were armed paramilitaries operating in the building that would affect the legitimacy of the decision to strike the building?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. However, it would probably, in my view, depend on what the reason behind it is. Is it actually to attack such units if they did exist or was it still a target to actually attack the television station itself? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, and I agree that we don't know at this stage that since no investigation was performed of that. But, sir, the question I have for you, as someone who has been trained by the Irish Defence Forces, and in the recitation of your background you talked about 30 years experience in the military, and you had several positions after the Irish Defence Forces: Would you agree with me that if a civilian building is being used by a hostile force to open fire upon another combatant, that that combatant is entitled to shoot back onto that location to neutralise the threat? Hypothetical, of course, but ...

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understand it's hypothetical, and I think I would probably need to have more information before I could give an answer on that, but basically I think I understand what you're getting at. On the one hand, you know, a -- a television station can be under certain circumstances a military target. It depends on what's coming out of the television station. On the other, it's a part of an institution of a state. So I think it probably would depend on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I think that's the best I can do for you on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's okay, sir -- Colonel. That's exactly where I stand as well. With respect to any military strikes, based upon your 30 years experience, would you agree with me that all the care and technology in the world cannot completely eliminate the prospect of civilian damage or casualties that result from an otherwise legitimate military target being struck?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm getting a little bit confused. Could you -- could you just repeat that for me, please, until I give it some consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like we're now in a legal discourse. Don't we talk of collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And isn't that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking, Your Honours. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the great focuses or one of the great problems we have in the military is the whole issue of collateral damage, and of course in recent years and in recent conflicts it's become more and more to the fore. We only have to think of the collateral damage done to a premises in Belgrade. However, that's why I find it just difficult to -- to side one way or the other on an issue of this nature. But I would agree that an order for an attack on a premises, one would want to be fairly sure that you're going about it the right way and it's for a legitimate reason and that it is a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can have just one more document that I believe you -- I believe this one you haven't seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this one -- the 17th Partisan Brigade document I will not -- also not be seeking to tender as an exhibit at this time. If we can call up, Madam Registrar, 1D00169.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, as we wait for that to come up, I can preface my remarks by saying that we will see that is a 11 May 1992 report of the Ilidza police station, and if we go to the fourth page in the Serbian and the second page in the English, I think we will see this selection that also talks about the Sarajevo -- the RTV building. And Colonel, if I can direct your attention to the part that begins, and I quote: "We have acquired information that in the RTV Sarajevo building, a large number of Green Berets are present daily; that is, there are 50 to 70 of them there at all times. They are led by Sejo Saric, who had worked in the security services of this building previously. The requisitor known as Boca is also one of the leaders and is also very extreme. A group of the reserve police and Territorial Defence (TO) are commanded by a certain Saban Sljem with the help of Bajrovic and some Kasim. Among them are snipers Zeljko Jandric and Zoran Milovanovic, specialists of the former MUP. They are armed with automatic weapons, machine-guns, portable launchers, and bazookas. They carry a large quantity of ammunition. During the attack on Svrakino Selo, 30 to 40 members of the Green Berets had arrived on the property of the TV station. Portable launchers and bazookas are being placed on top of the TV station by which they could fire at ranges up to 500 metres. We have been told that their combat morale is not at a high level, which is particularly visible prior to the bombing of the building." And now, Colonel, first of all, the standard question: Am I correct that this information was not known to you or available to you prior to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, I'll just ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, there is no relevance to whether the information was known to him unless the information was true. So he should be asking any knowledge that there were, in fact, Green Berets in the building not -- not presupposing again that the information is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, what is wrong with the question was the information -- the information was not available to you? That's the question put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think the question as worded -- it's ambiguous whether he's asking -- if he answers "yes," it would be ambiguous on the record as to whether he's saying -- sorry, if he answers "no," it would be ambiguous on the record as to whether he's saying, No the information was never conveyed to me, or he is not given an opportunity to say, Well, in fact -- to disagree with the information that's being put to him if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether the -- whether counsel intends to put the case to him, whether he disagrees with it. All he wants to know is did you have this information at the time. And the question [sic] is yes I did or no I did not. I don't think there can be any ambiguity about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, no, the answer -- the question as worded, Your Honour, was was this information -- sorry. I think "conveyed" I think it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is -- let's read it as it was put: "And now Colonel, first of all, the standard question, am I correct that this information was not known to you or available to you prior to ..." And then you objected. Yes, it was not available to me; no, you are wrong, it was available to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. I -- I think the question is ambiguous in my mind, Your Honour, but clearly you disagree and there is no point in belabouring the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Put the question, sir, exactly as it was put.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that this information was not available to you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And without getting into whether the matters asserted are accurate and true or not, because neither you nor I can do that at this point, I want to ask you: Would you agree with me that to reach an accurate picture of the truth, these allegations of a building being used to set up offensive weapons would have to be fully looked into before assessing the legitimacy of a strike on a building?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would. But I should state here that I was warned in advance by Serbs that they were going to bomb the station if they did not close it down. They did not say to me, We will bomb this station if this or that. That was the specific. And I brought that personally to the attention of Mr. Karadzic who assured me that it would not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's all in your statement in the paragraph that I referenced --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- at the beginning. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will also not be seeking to tender this, Your Honour, so we can remove that from e-court for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, I wish to move onto another topic. In paragraph 79 of your statement, you do talk about a battle that took place just outside of your hotel which you eye-witnessed. Am I correct, first, that the -- that your hotel is near the area where the TV building we have been talking about is located?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not beside it. It would be some kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this combat that you saw, I -- I -- strike that. I shouldn't say combat. You refer to it as a battle. This battle that you saw on the 22nd of April, 1992, am I correct that the armed Bosnian Muslim forces were the antagonists; that is to say, the attacking or offensive party?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assessment was that it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And one other clarification as to this incident. In your statement, you mention that 13 persons were killed. Do you recall if these were civilians or combatants?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information was given to me by a reporter from the BBC who was on the ground. I saw some bodies. The ones that I saw were in uniform -- sorry. They were in paramilitary uniform. They were in the uniform that was worn by police. I understood them to be Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if we go to one other item from your statement. In paragraph 87, you mention a letter that, in fact, is Annex 9 to your statement but which we here in the courtroom now know as P94, I believe. 65 ter number 10980 and I believe it entered into court as P94. This is a letter written by the mayor of Sarajevo, and while we wait for that to come up on the screen I would ask you: Do you recall this letter?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And very briefly on this, and I will rest assured as I have done all yesterday and today, I will give you a fair opportunity to get everything that you've said about this letter in there. Can I first just remind that you testified in the Milosevic case that in your opinion this letter was probably overstated. Is that an accurate -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was my assessment that there were some exaggerations in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to be fair to you, sir, I wish to also read the remainder of what you said about this letter so that everything is out there, and this is from the Milosevic -- the Slobodan Milosevic case, transcript page 25354, lines 14 to 21, and it's -- I believe you will be able to follow along. It's brief. "What I would say about that is that in lots of reports that I got from all sides there was the general tendency to exaggerate and this, in my view, was one of those. I do not in any way dispute the fact that the situation was getting pretty desperate and that there was an urgent need for corridors to be opened to get humanitarian aid into the city, but from the experience I had in the former Yugoslavia over the 12 months, I would say that all the sides, from time to time, in my opinion, seemed to exaggerate the situation." And, sir, does that now complete your recollection on your stance as to this letter as [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if I can move onto another topic. I want to ask you about something that struck me in regards to the efforts of the negotiators in Lisbon. And here I'm talking about May 1992. Am I correct that you personally there Lisbon several days during this time-period, and in particular when the 27 May bread queue massacre occurred?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, I believe you were only questioned about that in the Slobodan Milosevic case. At least that's the only place where I found a reference to this item. Otherwise, I would have called up reports. But on the 26th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, is it on now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's on now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't know that the Slobodan Milosevic transcript was included on my friend's document list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can refresh counsel's recollection, it's included on their exhibit list and my list says I may use anything on the Prosecution's exhibit list. It's listed under prior testimony, Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic, case number IT-02-54-T, 26 and 27 August 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Bolton. Yes, Mr. Ivetic. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I will read to you again, as I have, the entirety of what you are recorded as having said there, and then I'll ask the questions thereafter and you will be free to clarify, add to, or correct anything. Again, this is the 26th of August 2003 at transcript page 25299, line 19, going to transcript page 25300, line 10. And I begin with your -- with -- with -- with what was there. "A short time after that Radovan Karadzic was very anxious to come in and talk with us, and we had a discussion about meeting with him. So when he came in, immediately -- he immediately inferred that the Bosnian Serbs were not responsible for that mortar. I recall Ambassador Cutileiro saying to him, asking him how was he -- how did he know that this attack could not be attributed to the Bosnian Serbs because it was impossible to have contact with Sarajevo from Lisbon. However, what was attempted by the conference, as a result of this, was that Dr. Karadzic was informed that whether the Serbs were to blame or not, they, the Serbs, were actually responsible for it or not, they probably were going to be blamed, and, therefore, it would be the interest of them to make a gesture to our conference. We had discussed this previously to Dr. Karadzic coming in, and I suggested - I think it was I; I may not be sure on that - but one of us suggested that maybe we exploit this to be able to get an agreement on the airport. So after some considerable time, Dr. Karadzic agreed that in certain circumstances he would be willing to hand over control of Sarajevo airport to the United Nations." Colonel, have I accurately recited --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the incident in question is the bread queue explosion at Vasa Miskina street that is commonly referred to as the first of the Markale attacks?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that a forensic investigation later determined that the Bosnian Muslim forces were likely responsible for this incident?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that. That's my understanding, that the United Nations crater analysis was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought there was an issue with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you don't allow it, then I will move on. But the question I have for you is is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Bolton is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone. It's on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My notes actually do indicate that there may an error on the transcript on that line as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The answer: "I have no knowledge of that. That's my understanding, that the United Nations crater analysis was different." I think the witness had said something close to that, but no, my information was that the UN crater analysis -- sorry, was different. And there's something missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would happy to let the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- re-answer that. I think that's the safest way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know personally what the definitive decision on that was. I do know that the United Nations carried out a crater analysis. But not being a member of the United Nations, I don't know what that was. So I can't say for definite who fired that mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir.
