Would this example from Lisbon, would it -- from this, can we -- can we conclude that in a desire to fulfil the mission objectives, international negotiators from the European Community sometimes had to operate in this manner to try to assess blame without knowing the full answer yet to try and get some concessions from various parties in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And then I have one other area also related to the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to 1D00170.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, when this comes up, if I can direct your attention to the last paragraph of this document, and I will wait for it to come up. And, again, sir, is this a document that you recognise as one that you authored?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I haven't read it yet, but it bears my signature all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you want, we can have it returned to the first page. Would that be --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could have the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, when you've have had an opportunity to review, if you could just confirm whether in fact this is a document that you recall having been authored by you.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see where the document has my signature and authorisation, but I actually don't -- I don't recall that -- that -- that actual report. Could I -- could I just quickly see page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Definitely, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we show the witness the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I'll give you some time to review that.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It bears my signature and I would have to say that I did sign it. But I'm -- I'm a little bit -- I'm a little bit curious as to why it refers to coming from Belgrade on the first page. I'm -- I'm just not sure on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Nor am I, sir. In any event, do you -- do you recognise the subject matter of the -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. I'm only interested in one aspect of this and I will put it to you and you're free to comment on it, if it is or is not something you recall authoring. If I can look to the last paragraph of this document, the last -- actually, I'm not seeing the part that I'm looking for. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you looking for the last paragraph on the second page or on the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the last -- the last -- it's supposed to be the last paragraph on the last page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the last page? Well, there is the last paragraph: Kind regards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's not what I have written here. One moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me see if the witness recalls this text before we spend more time looking for it. Sir, I have listed here that in this document there is a paragraph that begins as follows: "There is a strong body of opinion to suggest" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First page. I apologise then. The last paragraph of the first page. That's it. Thank you, Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, here we can read along now: "There is a strong body of opinion to suggest that the Muslims would be happy if the airport was not made operational as this would decrease the chances of they (the Muslims) achieving the objective of getting some sort of military intervention. There seems to be a greater determination on the part of the Serbs to open the airport." Now, do you recall this specific portion of this correspondence that was -- that is before you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I understand what the reason behind that paragraph would have been, yes, my understanding. Because, at that time, the -- the Muslims or the SDA were very -- at the Presidency, specifically the president was very anxious to try and get military intervention in -- and an indication that the situation might be somehow returning to normal would be opening up the airport. So politically speaking this would have been something that they would have preferred not to have happened. That would have been my judgement and that's -- I would accept that's why I would have put it down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and that's how I understood it and I'm glad for the added explanation. If I can just ask a follow-up on that. Would you agree with me that this overarching desire to try to seek military intervention from the outside, i.e., from the United States or NATO, that this was exhibited by the SDA leadership not only in regards to the airport but with regards to other negotiations that you were a party to or have knowledge of during the time-period that you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't actually say that it was. But I do know that politically the SDA wanted to have military intervention as a means of bringing the war to a conclusion. That was my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour -- thank you, Colonel. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And one moment. Let me just check one thing, Your Honours. I think I'm done with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel, I do have one follow-up question. It's with regard to the uniforms of the dead -- of the dead casualties that you saw from the gun battle outside of your hotel in April of 1992. How -- could you -- could you illuminate for us how it is that you were able to determine the uniforms in question to identify them as being paramilitary uniforms worn by the police?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- when that, I suppose battle, or outbreak of fighting occurred, when I looked out the window, the first thing I saw was a Serb half-track coloured blue and white which was the colours, and the uniforms were also blue, and they were the uniforms that were being worn by the police at that stage. The fact that it was a Serb area, the fact that Muslims had already had been moved out of the area was a clear indication to me as to what was happening. And, therefore, it was my assumption that the people who were defending the area were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Colonel, I thank you for your time and your patience. I have no further questions for you and I thank you for the answers that you have given.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ivetic. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I do have a brief re-examination of the witness. May I just have a moment to organise my papers. May I begin, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can I have on the screen, please, 65 ter 10943.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is a document you were asked about yesterday by my friend. In particular, you were asked about a note that appears at the end of the document, which is -- will be the next page, where you express some concerns about the legality of the referendum and, in particular, you indicated there was some concerns about the legality of the assembly being reconvened after it was closed by the assembly president and also the authority of the president of the assembly to conclude the session without a majority in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm wondering if we could please go back to the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Under item 10, there's an indication, it says -- before the list there's an indication most of the speakers during the debate were from the SDS party, all of whom opposed the holding of a referendum with various arguments of which the following were the main points. And then point 10 is: "Recommend that SDA/HDZ go ahead without SDS as they (SDS) already had a plebescite on November 9th/10th." And my question is: What are they referring "go ahead" without the SDS?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead with the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now you told us yesterday that it was the position of the Bosnian Serbs that the requirement for the referendum required that it be done in order to have a legitimate vote on the referendum that required that there be a consensus amongst all three ethnic groups and not just a simple parliamentary majority is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that after they provided that information to you that you went and spoke to some judges at the supreme court of Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was that in an informal manner or was this a formal court case that you brought?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was an initiative on my part.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And to the best of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was an initiative on your part, Mr. Doyle, but was it a formal or an informal initiative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It followed a request I made. I was trying to clarify this whole issue, so I asked if I could meet some of the more legally qualified people of the state, and I was told, yes, this will happen, and I was told where to go at what time and I met them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The short answer is it was an informal --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been. I beg your pardon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, sir, did anyone from the SDS or anyone associated with the Bosnian Serb people ever initiate an action in the Bosnian supreme court to get a formal ruling from the court as to the legality or illegality of that vote?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can answer that best by explaining that when arrived for that meeting, the deputy minister of justice, who was a Serb, asked me what it was I wanted to address with these judges. And when I mentioned I was trying to get an official legal interpretation of this whole issue, and he said that's not open for discussion. So I waited until he left, and then I had the discussion that I wanted. And what I was told by one of the judges is, Mr. Doyle, you're looking for something that is impossible to define, because we judges could from different ethnic backgrounds, so what I will tell you, for example, as a member, as a judge who is a Muslim will be different to what you will be told by a judge who is a Serb. So I left that meeting rather frustrated because I felt if I couldn't get a definitive answer by the highest legal powers in the state, if they couldn't themselves agree as to what was and what wasn't constitutional or legal, then it was going to be very difficult to get a definitive answer. So I recall that and that's why I put that in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And your answer was just slightly different from my question which was --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether there was ever any court proceeding actually initiated by the SDS to get an actual ruling from the court, a formal ruling?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page of this document again, please. And to the bottom of the page under: "Comments." There is an indication under comment 1 that you remarked that the presence of the SDS at that session was for cosmetic purposes. What you did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impression that I got at the time was that the SDS members were going to object regardless of what came up. Once it appears to me that they had decided in advance that they will not vote anything towards a referendum, and if they stick with that line, going on the basis of consensus, then no decision could be made.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That ends my questions on this document, Your Honours, and I note that the witness has been asked extensively about it in cross-examination and now by myself in re-examination, and I think it should be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10943 becomes Exhibit P100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At page 1560 of the transcript yesterday, Defence counsel suggested to you that the only person you spoke to in the Bosnian Presidency who expressed view -- the view that -- only -- that -- sorry. If the referendum was successful that the Bosnian Serbs wouldn't be happy but they'd come to accept it was President Izetbegovic. And I'm wondering if you could refer to paragraph 54 of your statement where you indicate that -- you were asked to approach the various party leaders and that you spoke with President Izetbegovic, Vice-President Ganic, Foreign Minister Silajdzic, and Radovan Karadzic. And then you say: "The members of the Bosnian Presidency all said the same thing. They said they believed the Bosnian Serbs would not be happy with this recognition but they would come around to accept it with time." Does that refresh your memory as to whether it was just President Izetbegovic who expressed that view?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I should explain here that the person who spoke to me personally about it was President Izetbegovic, but at the time he did it I was at a meeting in which -- which was also attended by Haris Silajdzic, who's the foreign minister, and Ejup Ganic. So it was actually the president who said the words of the opinion of the SDA. I apologise if there was any confusion about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have ID002148, please. I understand it may come up under the number 1D00173. And may I have page -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: First you're looking at the first page, and you recognise this as the witness statement Defence counsel referred to yesterday as being from Mr. Halilovic. Sorry, do you remember being asked about this yesterday, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 26 in e-court, please. When -- and if we could have the top of the page, please, the witness statement portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you were being asked questions yesterday by Defence counsel, he referred to this statement as the sworn statement of General Sefer Halilovic, and I'd ask you to read the top portion of this document under "Witness Statement," and then I will have a question for you. Just read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you see any reference to the witness being administered an oath before he provided this statement?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the witness is advised, however, that he may be assisted by an attorney, if he so desires?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And he is cautioned that: "There's an investigation in progress into events in Bosnia-Herzegovina during which period of time he held command responsibility within the Bosnian army and that the investigation may subsequently bring out facts which might involve my own responsibility."

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were you -- or are you aware of whether General Halilovic was in fact ever indicted or tried by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 28 in this document in e-court, please. There's a reference at the very first paragraph. If we could go to the top of the page, please. Thank you. To a meeting of 2nd December 1991. And you were asked ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Court's indulgence. And then if we could scroll to the bottom of this same page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Another segment that was put you to was the very last paragraph here which reads: "It was obvious that the war was unavoidable." And it talks about their efforts to try to secure weapons quickly at that time. Do you have any personal knowledge of what efforts were being made by the Bosnians to secure weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It was suggested to you in questions yesterday that the Muslims were buying weapons on the black market and that this was being done with money being obtained from the Middle East. Do you have any knowledge as to whether or not that was true?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Or whether they expended millions of dollars on such equipment?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And whether or not President Izetbegovic personally authorised that work?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you have any idea as to when those -- sorry, I withdraw that question. You were asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm done with this document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before the document leaves I would like -- can we scroll up, please. I would like to take particular note of the second paragraph from the top and ask for your comment if you have any, Mr. Doyle, particularly the sentence that says: "It," the national Defence committee, which was the basis for the formation of the Patriotic League, "It consisted of an alliance of all the Bosnian patriotic forces regardless of cultural, ethnic, or religious origins." Do you have any comment to make on that in the light of questions put to you yesterday about the ethnicity of the membership of the league?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be -- if we're talking about it being under the control of the SDA, or Muslims, the sentence saying: "It consisted of an allegiance of all Bosnian patriotic forces regardless of cultural, ethnic, or religious origins," that seems to be -- to be a contradiction in terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document may get off.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were asked some questions today about the fact that that the barracks in Sarajevo -- or at least one barracks in Sarajevo was surrounded on May 2nd, 1992. You recall that line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you have any information or knowledge as to what the purpose was of surrounding the barracks?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't have any detailed knowledge as to why it occurred, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, how much longer are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were asked today about a report from the area of -- I want to pronounce it Neum, N-e-u-m, about Croatian forces on Bosnian soil. Other than in that area, did you have any other reports of Croatian forces on Bosnian soil?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, all of the forces were confined to western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in terms of -- you were asked about public proclamations by the European Community condemning the presence of Croatian troops on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and you said you weren't aware of any. Were you aware of whether the United Nations Security Council ever issued any statements or resolutions in regards to the matter?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You told us -- in response to some questions today, my friend suggested -- had some questions about your conversation with General Ninkovic when he relayed the message that you wouldn't be allowed by General Mladic to the area of the 9th Corps. If I could refer you to paragraph 37 of your statement, there's an indication there that you had a meeting with General Ninkovic, and you -- I take it, at the 10th Corps in Bihac on the 17th of January, 1992. Do you recall whether the information about General Mladic not allowing access was conveyed at that meeting or another meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my understanding it was at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were asked some questions today about paramilitary forces in the TV building in Sarajevo. Did you have occasion to actually be inside the TV building in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was frequently there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you were in the building, did you ever see signs of any military installations?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge. I did not see any armed forces in the television building.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Any weapons?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where is the TV building relative to the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's pretty close. I can't remember exactly, but certainly within half a kilometre. Could be even closer. I can't now remember. But it was during the period that I used to visit the United Nations who were based in the PTT building, so it wasn't very hard -- it wasn't that far from the television station.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you were having the talks about the JNA withdrawal from the barracks in May 1992, where were they held?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were held in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you ever hear any outgoing fire from -- or see any outgoing fire from the TV building --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- during those talks?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those are all my questions. I thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Bolton. Mr. Doyle, thank you so much for coming to the Tribunal to testify. We've now come to the conclusion of your testimony. You may now stand down. You are released. And may you travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I realise we are approaching the time for the break. I do have important information with respect to the next witness, that's witness's ability to proceed this afternoon. If we have a few moments, I can update the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just prior to the start of this session, a representative of the victim and witnesses services asked to speak with me and informed me that a chronic medical condition of RM115 had been exacerbated. Over the course of this session, we've now been informed that it has become acute and the witness has been returned to the hotel room. I stepped out of the chamber around 11.30 to see if I could organise or advance the witness -- one of the witnesses from next week, and that is proving impossible. So it seems that there are no witnesses that we can call to the stand this afternoon. I apologise for that, but it is an unforeseen event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Quite understandable. Thank you so much for that update. In that event, can we stay a little longer so that we do some housekeeping matters before we break for the day. First of all, I just wanted to ask the Prosecution, I -- yes, Madam Bolton, asking you, with respect to P99 MFI, have you been able to get a B/C/S translation? It was MFI'd yesterday because of the translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm advised that it is not yet available but it should be available later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can you remember on Monday then, to make sure that -- or ask whoever from you comes to court --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart will remember on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Stewart. The next point, there is an oral decision that the Chamber would like to render. Actually, it's not a decision. These are reasons for a decision and a decision. I'm going to correct myself one more time. They're reasons for a decision and a decision. Okay. Reasons for decision on Prosecution motion for leave to file an amended Rule 65 ter summary for Witness RM147 and decision on the amendments to the Rule 65 ter summaries of Witnesses RM039 and RM078. The Chamber will now deliver the reason for its decisions granting the Prosecution motion for leave to file an amended Rule 65 ter summary for Witness RM147 and denying the Defence request to postpone hearing of this witness's testimony which was informally communicated to the parties on 20 July 2012. It will also deliver its decision with regard to the Rule 65 ter summaries for Witnesses RM039 and RM078. In this respect, the Chamber grants the Prosecution's request for leave to reply with regard to Witness RM078 filed on the 22nd August 2012. On the 11th of June, 2012, the Prosecution requested leave to amend its Rule 65 ter witness summary for this witness so as to include additional information arising from a proofing session held on the 2nd and 3rd of June, 2012 concerning primarily the alleged shelling of Sarajevo on the 28th and 29th May 1992, as described in Scheduled Incident G1 of the indictment. The new information was set out in a consolidated witness statement signed by the witness on 3 June and disclosed to the Defence on the 8th of June, 2012. The Prosecution submitted that the sought amendment to the witness's Rule 65 ter summary would be consistent with the interests of justice and would cause no prejudice to the accused, Mr. Mladic. On the 25th of June, 2012, the Defence requested that the motion be denied as the proposed amendments sought to change material aspects of the witness's testimony and caused, as such, undue prejudice to the Defence. In the alternative, requested that the testimony of Witness RM147 be delayed by 90 days so as to allow adequate time for the Defence to prepare for his testimony. The Chamber emphasises that the purpose of Rule 65 ter witness summaries is to notify the opposing party and the Chamber of the content of evidence expected to be elicited from a witness. Such notice should be given sufficiently in advance of a witness's testimony so as to enable the opposing party to prepare for the witness's cross-examination. The amendment sought for Witness RM147's Rule 65 ter summary concerned information which was included in the consolidated witness statement that was disclosed to the Defence on the 8th of June, 2012 and in the Prosecution's 11th of June, 2012 motion. As such, the Chamber considered that the Defence had been on notice of the Prosecution's intention to lead the proposed additional evidence sufficiently in advance of the witness's testimony which is scheduled for the week of the 27th of August, 2012. The Defence did not sufficiently demonstrate that the witness's testimony would need to be delayed due to the additional information to be elicited. For similar reasons, the Chamber allows the requested amendments to the Rule 65 ter summaries concerning Witnesses RM039 and RM078. The requests, which specify the information sought to be added to the relevance summaries, place the Defence sufficiently on notice of the evidence the Prosecution intends to elicit from these witnesses. As for the Defence submission that parts of the transcript of a past testimony of Witness RM078 have not been disclosed by the Prosecution, the Chamber notes that it appears that the relevant pages of the transcript have been disclosed and, in any event, are publicly available on the Tribunal's web site. The Chamber would like to provide the parties with general guidance with regard to amendments to the Rule 65 ter witness summaries. It considers that, in principle, the parties do not need to seek leave to amend these summaries. It is sufficient to provide the opposing party and the Chamber with adequate notice of such amendments as soon as possible, and, in any event, sufficiently in advance of the witness's testimony. Should the opposing party consider that eliciting the new information would cause undue prejudice, it may request the calling party to reschedule the testimony of the witness concerned or seek any other appropriate relief from the Chamber. This concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision concerning RM147 and its oral decision on the amendments to the Rule 65 ter summaries of Witnesses RM039 and RM078. Are there any housekeeping matter that any of the parties has? Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- the only housekeeping matter that the Prosecution would seek to raise is -- or just ask the Chamber, since RM147 is scheduled to testify next week, if we could have some information when we might expect some decisions. There are a few pending applications with respect to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sitting where I am, I can say as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is not very helpful, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Mr. Lukic, anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Defence has nothing to raise at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Well, in that case ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We were, in any case, going to tell you what we were saying. Is the Prosecution in a position to tell the Chamber and the Defence whether the witness who was not able to testify today will be able to testify on Monday, or -- and/or if not, whether you are able to have an alternative witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, RM147 was a witness that has some restrictions on their availability, and that is the witness that we have scheduled for Monday. So what we would propose to do is proceed on Monday with RM147. The witness who became ill today, RM115, if that witness returns to good health, then we would call that witness immediately after that. And then proceed with Mr. Jordan after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do I therefore understand that you want these decisions before Monday? These pending decisions with respect to RM147.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Or at least informal communication so we can prepare the witness and can finalize our preparations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. In that event, we stand adjourned to Monday morning, 9.00 -- 9.30 in Courtroom I. Am I right? Thank you so much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of August, 2012, at 9.30 a.m.
